title: The Coercion Trap
text:
At the Oregon Social Learning Center in Eugene, the psychologist Gerald Patterson and his colleagues spent years observing families of aggressive and hard-to-manage children, often in their own homes. Trained observers sat quietly in the living room and recorded, every few seconds, what each family member did and how the others responded.

Patterson saw the same sequence again and again. A parent asked a child to do something, like turning off the television. The child whined, argued or yelled. The parent, worn down, gave up. The child had just learned that being unpleasant works. But the parent had also learned something: giving in made the whining stop at once, which felt like relief.

The pattern could also run the other way. When the parent finally exploded and shouted, the child often complied, which taught the parent that yelling worked. Over thousands of such small exchanges, parent and child trained each other into longer and harsher conflicts. Patterson called it coercive family process and described it in a 1982 book of that name.

The insight was practical. His team developed parent management training, which teaches parents to give clear, calm instructions, follow through with mild and consistent consequences, and notice and reward good behavior. It became one of the best-supported treatments for children's conduct problems.
lesson: Giving in to whining and winning by yelling both teach bad habits. Calm, consistent follow-through and attention to good behavior break the cycle.
location: Oregon Social Learning Center, Eugene, USA
source: Patterson, G. R. (1982). Coercive Family Process. Eugene, OR: Castalia.
